radar-001.question: In a pulsed radar, the time from transmitting a pulse to receiving the target echo is 200 µs. What is the range to the target? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
radar-001.explanation: The wave travels from the radar to the target and back, so the measured time is the round-trip time. The range is R = ct/2 = 3×10⁸ × 200×10⁻⁶/2 = 3×10⁴ m, or 30 km. 60 km forgets to divide by 2 and gives the round-trip distance. 15 km divides by 2 once too often. As a rule of thumb, 1 µs of delay corresponds to 150 m of range in radar. This round-trip idea is the source of the factor of 1/2 in many radar formulas, such as the range resolution (cτ/2) and the maximum unambiguous range (c/(2·PRF)).

radar-002.question: Which is closest to the range resolution (the smallest range difference at which two targets in the same direction can be seen as separate echoes) of a pulsed radar using an unmodulated rectangular pulse 1 µs wide? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
radar-002.explanation: When two targets differ in range by ΔR, their echoes differ in time by 2ΔR/c because of the round trip. If this time difference is shorter than the pulse width τ, the two echoes overlap and look like one, so the range resolution is ΔR = cτ/2 = 3×10⁸ × 10⁻⁶/2 = 150 m. 300 m uses cτ, ignoring the round trip. 75 m divides by 2 again. Finer range resolution could be had with shorter pulses, but a shorter pulse carries less energy, making distant targets harder to see. Pulse compression resolves this conflict.

radar-003.question: Which correctly describes the effect of pulse compression (such as a chirp, in which the frequency changes linearly within the pulse) in pulsed radar?
choices: It avoids raising the peak power, but the range resolution, set by the pulse length, becomes coarse
It makes the Doppler frequency zero, so even moving targets can be located accurately
It gains energy from a long pulse while making the range resolution about c/(2B), set by the signal bandwidth B
radar-003.explanation: In pulse compression, a long pulse carrying frequency modulation (a chirp) or a phase code is transmitted, and a matched filter at the receiver compresses it into a short pulse. The compressed pulse width is about 1/B, so the range resolution is set by c/(2B) regardless of the original pulse length. A long pulse can deliver a lot of energy, so fine range resolution is obtained while securing detection range without raising peak power. Resolution set by the transmitted pulse length applies to simple unmodulated pulses. The Doppler frequency is a physical effect set by the target's velocity, so pulse compression cannot make it zero; with a chirp, coupling between range and velocity (range-Doppler coupling) can even introduce an error.

radar-004.question: In a pulsed radar with a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 2 kHz, at what range is the echo from a target actually 100 km away displayed? The radar calculates range from the delay after the most recently transmitted pulse; take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
choices: It is not displayed (echoes from targets beyond the maximum unambiguous range are not received)
radar-004.explanation: The maximum unambiguous range is Ru = c/(2·PRF) = 3×10⁸/(2 × 2000) = 75 km. The echo from a target at 100 km returns about 667 µs after transmission, but the pulse interval is 500 µs, so it arrives about 167 µs after the next pulse. The radar treats it as an echo of the most recent pulse, so it is displayed at 100 − 75 = 25 km (a second-time-around or second-trace echo). The correct 100 km display occurs only if the target is within 75 km. Echoes from distant targets are received if they are strong enough, so "not displayed" is wrong; the problem is that they appear as false, nearby targets. One remedy is to switch the PRF and find the true range from how the apparent range changes.

radar-005.question: Which correctly describes the effect of raising the pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of a pulse-Doppler radar?
choices: The maximum unambiguous range gets shorter, and the range of Doppler frequencies (velocities) that can be measured unambiguously gets wider
Both the maximum unambiguous range and the range of Doppler frequencies (velocities) that can be measured unambiguously get wider
The maximum unambiguous range gets longer, and the range of Doppler frequencies (velocities) that can be measured unambiguously gets narrower
radar-005.explanation: The maximum unambiguous range is c/(2·PRF), so raising the PRF shortens it. Meanwhile, a pulse-Doppler radar finds the Doppler frequency from the pulse-to-pulse phase change of the echoes, which amounts to sampling at the PRF, so the Doppler frequencies that can be measured unambiguously extend only to ±PRF/2. Raising the PRF widens this range. Range and velocity ambiguity are therefore traded off against each other through the PRF, and both cannot be widened at once. Low PRF, which favors long unambiguous range; high PRF, which favors velocity; and medium PRF in between are chosen according to the application. The option corresponding to lowering the PRF has the direction backward.

radar-006.question: A target approaches a 24 GHz Doppler radar head-on at 25 m/s (90 km/h). Which is closest to the Doppler frequency of the echo? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
radar-006.explanation: The wavelength is λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/(24×10⁹) = 12.5 mm. In radar the wave travels to the target and back, so it undergoes the Doppler effect both ways, and the Doppler frequency is fd = 2v/λ = 2 × 25/0.0125 = 4000 Hz, or 4 kHz. 2 kHz forgets the factor of 2, giving v/λ, the value for a wave traveling one way, as in communications. 14.4 kHz is a unit error, plugging in the km/h figure of 90. An approaching target raises the echo frequency, and a receding one lowers it. By measuring this Doppler frequency, which is proportional to velocity, a radar directly obtains the target's radial velocity.

radar-007.question: A target moves at right angles to the line of sight of a Doppler radar (the line joining the radar and the target). Which statement about the observed Doppler frequency is correct?
choices: It is proportional to the target's speed itself
It is proportional to twice the target's speed and is larger than for an approaching target
radar-007.explanation: Only a change in the distance between the target and the radar — the velocity component along the line of sight — produces a Doppler frequency. With speed v and angle θ to the line of sight, fd = 2v cos θ/λ; at θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so the Doppler frequency is nearly zero. It is proportional to the speed itself only when the target moves along the line of sight (θ = 0°). Because a target crossing at right angles produces no Doppler frequency however fast it moves, radars that reject echoes near zero Doppler as stationary clutter such as the ground may also reject crossing targets, making them hard to see. In automotive radar too, the velocity of a crossing car is hard to obtain from a single measurement, so the change in angle is tracked to compensate.

radar-008.question: Which correctly describes the difference between a Doppler radar transmitting a constant-frequency continuous wave (unmodulated CW) and an FMCW radar whose frequency changes linearly with time?
choices: An unmodulated CW radar can measure range from the transmit-receive phase difference but, with no Doppler frequency, cannot measure velocity
Both are continuous waves with no time marker like a pulse, so neither the Doppler frequency nor the delay time can be measured
An unmodulated CW radar can measure velocity but not range, while an FMCW radar uses the frequency change as a time marker to measure range too
radar-008.explanation: A constant-frequency continuous wave carries no marker of when it was sent, so the echo delay — the range — cannot be determined. The Doppler frequency can still be measured as the frequency difference between the received and transmitted waves, so such radars are used where only speed is needed, as in speed guns. An FMCW radar changes its frequency linearly (a chirp), so the transmit frequency changes while the echo is returning, and the difference (the beat frequency) is proportional to the delay. This lets a continuous wave measure range, and using multiple chirps gives velocity as well. "Range but not velocity" is backward, and "neither" overlooks that a frequency change can serve as a time marker even without pulses.

radar-009.question: An FMCW radar sweeps its frequency linearly by 300 MHz in 50 µs (a slope of 6×10¹² Hz/s). Which is closest to the beat frequency obtained by mixing the echo from a stationary target at 25 m with the transmitted wave? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
radar-009.explanation: The echo delay is the round-trip time, τ = 2R/c = 2 × 25/(3×10⁸) ≈ 1.67×10⁻⁷ s. During that time the transmit frequency advances at the slope S = 300 MHz/50 µs = 6×10¹² Hz/s, so the beat frequency is fb = S·τ = 6×10¹² × 1.67×10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.0×10⁶ Hz, or 1 MHz. 0.5 MHz takes the delay as the one-way R/c. 2 MHz applies the round-trip factor of 2 twice. The beat frequency is proportional to range, so when the received beat signal is analyzed with an FFT, the frequency axis directly becomes the range axis. For a moving target, the Doppler frequency is added to this.

radar-010.question: Which is closest to the range resolution of an FMCW radar whose frequency sweep (bandwidth) is 1 GHz? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
radar-010.explanation: The range resolution of an FMCW radar is set by the sweep bandwidth B: ΔR = c/(2B) = 3×10⁸/(2 × 10⁹) = 0.15 m, or 15 cm. To separate two targets, their beat frequencies must differ by at least the reciprocal of the observation time, 1/T; converted to range, this becomes c/(2B), independent of the sweep time T. 30 cm forgets the round-trip factor of 2, giving c/B. 7.5 cm divides by 2 again. This relation has the same form as the resolution of pulse compression: the wider the bandwidth, the finer the range resolution. Automotive millimeter-wave radars use the wide bandwidth of the 79 GHz band (up to 4 GHz) to separate nearby pedestrians and objects finely.

radar-011.question: Which statement about the radar cross section (RCS) of a target is correct?
choices: It always equals the physical projected area of the target seen from the direction of the incoming wave, regardless of shape
It is set only by the target's material (its conductivity) and does not depend at all on the viewing direction (aspect angle) or frequency
Even for one target it varies greatly with viewing direction and frequency, and often does not match the physical size
radar-011.explanation: The radar cross section σ expresses the power a target reflects back toward the radar as the area of a hypothetical target that would scatter the intercepted power equally in all directions; its unit is m² (often expressed in dBsm). It is set by shape, orientation, material and frequency. A flat metal plate, for example, has an enormous σ when viewed head-on, but it drops sharply when the plate is tilted only slightly. Some objects, like corner reflectors, have a large σ despite being small, while others, like stealth aircraft, have a small σ despite being large. The RCS matches the physical projected area only in limited cases, such as a metal sphere much larger than the wavelength (σ = πa²). The option saying it depends only on material overlooks how strongly shape and orientation matter.

radar-012.question: Suppose the maximum detection range of a radar is proportional to the fourth root of the radar cross section (from the radar equation). If a target's radar cross section becomes 20 dB (1/100) smaller, by roughly what factor does the maximum detection range change (all other conditions equal)?
radar-012.explanation: In the radar equation the received power is proportional to σ/R⁴, so for a fixed minimum detectable power, the maximum detection range is proportional to the fourth root of σ. If σ falls to 1/100, the maximum detection range becomes (1/100)^(1/4) = 1/√10 ≈ 0.32 times. In dB, the received power changes as 40 log₁₀ R, so 20 dB corresponds to 0.5 in log₁₀ R, and the range becomes 10^(−0.5) ≈ 0.32 times. 0.1 times uses the square root (as for one-way propagation, inversely proportional to R²), and 0.01 times assumes proportionality to σ. Because of the fourth root, making a target look smaller shrinks the detection range only slowly, and conversely, extending the detection range requires a large improvement in transmit power or sensitivity.

radar-013.question: With a radar antenna whose beamwidth (half-power beamwidth) is 2°, you want to distinguish two targets at the same range of 10 km by their difference in azimuth. Which is closest to the guideline for the separable cross-range spacing (beamwidth × range)?
radar-013.explanation: Angular resolution is set roughly by the antenna beamwidth; two targets at the same range cannot be distinguished if they are in the beam at the same time. The cross-range spacing is the beamwidth in radians times the range: 2° × π/180 ≈ 0.0349 rad, and 0.0349 × 10,000 m ≈ 349 m, about 350 m. About 20 km is a unit error, multiplying 2 × 10,000 m with the angle still in degrees. About 175 m uses half the beamwidth (1°). Beamwidth is roughly proportional to λ/D, so improving angular resolution requires a larger antenna or a higher frequency. The farther the range, the wider the cross-range spacing for the same angle, so distant targets are harder to separate.

radar-014.question: An automotive FMCW millimeter-wave radar transmits many short chirps at regular intervals and finds range by taking the FFT of each chirp's beat signal. Which is the correct way to find the target's relative velocity?
choices: From the beat frequency of a single chirp alone, treating the beat frequency as proportional to the relative velocity
From the phase difference of the beat signals between receive antennas, treating that phase difference as proportional to the relative velocity
From how fast the phase of the same range bin rotates from chirp to chirp, found by a second FFT across the sequence of chirps
radar-014.explanation: When the target moves, its range changes slightly from chirp to chirp, and the phase of the beat signal appearing in the same range bin rotates by 4πΔR/λ each time. A second FFT across the sequence of chirps (a 2D FFT, or range-Doppler processing) gives the rate of this phase rotation — the Doppler frequency — and hence the velocity. At millimeter waves the wavelength is only about 4 mm, so even a tiny movement changes the phase a lot, allowing accurate velocity measurement. The beat frequency of a single chirp mixes range and velocity, and with short chirps it is almost entirely the range component, so velocity cannot be separated from it alone. The phase difference between receive antennas gives the target's angle (azimuth), not its velocity.

radar-015.question: An automotive millimeter-wave radar uses three transmit antennas and four receive antennas in a MIMO configuration, with each transmit antenna's signal distinguishable at the receiver (by time division, for example). If all antennas are on a straight line, the receive antennas are spaced d apart, and the transmit antennas are spaced 4d apart, how many elements does the virtual receive array used for angle estimation have?
radar-015.explanation: In MIMO radar, the signals from each transmit antenna are separated in time or by code, and the receiver identifies which transmit antenna each signal came from. For each transmit-receive pair, the phase relationship is the same as for a single receive antenna located at the sum of the transmit and receive positions, so the virtual array has 3 × 4 = 12 elements. With the four receive antennas spaced d apart and the transmit antennas 4d apart, the 12 virtual elements line up evenly at spacing d without overlapping. 7 just adds the number of antennas, and 4 counts only the physical receive antennas. A large aperture is obtained from few real antennas, so angular resolution can be raised on a small circuit board.
